lines.text: The roofline. Is your code waiting on memory, or on math?
A core needs two things. First, bytes. They arrive from memory at some rate: that's bandwidth, bytes per second.
Second, arithmetic. The core adds and multiplies those numbers. Each add or multiply is one FLOP, and the core can do so many per second.
So which one runs out first? It comes down to a single number.
Take the Phase 0 sum. One float is four bytes, and it gets one add. One FLOP for four bytes: a quarter of a FLOP per byte.
Decode's matrix times vector. Each four-byte weight gets a multiply and an add. Two FLOPs for four bytes: half a FLOP per byte.
Prefill with thirty-two tokens reuses that same weight thirty-two times. Sixty-four FLOPs from the same four bytes: sixteen per byte.
FLOPs per byte. It's called arithmetic intensity: how much work each byte brings with it.
Now some made-up limits. Memory delivers thirty gigabytes per second. The core can do twenty-eight billion FLOPs per second.
At half a FLOP per byte, thirty gigabytes a second can only feed fifteen billion FLOPs a second.
The shorter bar is the limit. The core sits idle about half the time, waiting for bytes. That's memory-bound.
Now slide up to sixteen FLOPs per byte. Memory could feed four hundred and eighty.
Way more than the core can use. Now the core is the limit. That's compute-bound.
Do that for every possible work per byte, and plot it. Work per byte along the bottom, the best possible speed up the side.
On the left, more work per byte means more speed, because every byte brings more math with it. That's the bandwidth roof.
Then it hits the core's peak, and goes flat. That's the compute roof.
Where the two meet is the ridge. Left of it, memory-bound. Right of it, compute-bound.
Each step along both axes is ten times bigger. That's what keeps the slope a straight line.
Decode's matrix times vector lands here, low on the slope.
Prefill lands up here, on the flat roof.
Watch what happens if we double the core's speed. The flat roof rises. The decode dot doesn't move at all.
For decode, faster math doesn't help. Reading fewer bytes does.
Store each weight in four bits, and the same math needs about seven times fewer bytes. The dot slides right, and climbs the slope.
Until it meets the flat roof. From there, the math is the limit again. Where exactly that happens, we'll have to measure.
One last point. The Phase 0 sum, at a quarter of a FLOP per byte. Its roof is up here.
But we measured it way down here: point eight two billion FLOPs per second. Far below its roof.
A roof is a limit, not a promise. The sum wasn't waiting on memory. It was waiting on its own chain of adds.
A point under the roof means something else is slowing it down. Finding out what, is the skill.
So: work per byte decides which limit you hit.
Left of the ridge, memory is the limit. Decode lives there.
And the roof is only an upper bound. If you're below it, go find out why.
